title: US Supreme Court Lets $1.29 Billion Devas Lawsuit Against ISRO's Antrix Proceed
excerpt: The unanimous ruling reverses a Ninth Circuit dismissal, finding the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act does not require 'minimum contacts' to sue a foreign government's commercial arm in American courts.
body:
• The US Supreme Court unanimously ruled that Devas Multimedia's $1.29 billion enforcement lawsuit against ISRO's commercial arm Antrix Corporation can proceed in American courts
  • Justice Samuel Alito wrote that the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act does not require plaintiffs to show "minimum contacts" with the United States when suing a foreign state's instrumentality
  • The ruling reverses a 2023 Ninth Circuit decision that had dismissed the case on jurisdictional grounds, sending the dispute back for further proceedings
  • India's own courts have declared Devas a fraudulent entity and set aside the original ICC arbitration award — defenses Antrix can still raise on remand

US Supreme Court Opens Door for Devas Enforcement

The United States Supreme Court has unanimously ruled that a $1.29 billion arbitral award enforcement suit filed by Devas Multimedia and its Mauritius-based affiliate against India's Antrix Corporation can proceed in American courts. The decision, authored by Justice Samuel Alito, reverses a 2023 Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals judgment that had dismissed the case on jurisdictional grounds.

https://x.com/BarryMoore70635/status/2088594663502487903

At issue was whether Devas needed to demonstrate that Antrix, a government-owned Indian company and the commercial arm of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), had "minimum contacts" with the United States to establish personal jurisdiction under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA).

"Personal jurisdiction exists under the FSIA when an immunity exception applies and service is proper. Because the Ninth Circuit required more, we reverse the judgment below."

— Justice Samuel Alito, writing for the Court

A Satellite Deal Gone Wrong

The dispute traces back to January 2005, when Antrix entered an agreement with Devas Multimedia, a Bengaluru-based startup, to lease transponders on two ISRO satellites. The arrangement would have enabled Devas to offer satellite-based multimedia services across India using S-band spectrum.

In 2011, the Indian government unilaterally cancelled the agreement, citing national security concerns and the need to reserve the S-band spectrum for strategic purposes. Devas initiated arbitration proceedings before the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), alleging wrongful repudiation of the contract. In 2015, the ICC tribunal awarded Devas $562.5 million in damages, which with interest grew to approximately $1.2 billion.

Parallel Legal Battles Across Continents

The case has played out simultaneously in Indian and American courts with starkly different outcomes. India's National Company Law Tribunal ordered the liquidation of Devas in 2021, calling it a sham entity, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court of India in 2022. The Delhi High Court separately set aside the ICC award, ruling that the Devas-Antrix deal was "entered into with a fraudulent intention."

Meanwhile, Devas sought enforcement of the ICC award in US courts. A district court initially confirmed the award, but the Ninth Circuit reversed on the grounds that Antrix lacked sufficient connections to the US to support personal jurisdiction.

What the Ruling Means

The Supreme Court disagreed with the Ninth Circuit's reasoning. Justice Alito emphasized that the FSIA was designed to provide a comprehensive and predictable framework for suing foreign states in the US. The Act's immunity exceptions — including the "direct effect" standard for commercial activity — already contain built-in requirements that address due process concerns, making an additional "minimum contacts" test unnecessary.

"Notably absent from the provision is any reference to 'minimum contacts.' And the Court declines to add what Congress left out," the judgment stated.

The Road Ahead

While the ruling clears a jurisdictional hurdle for Devas, it does not settle the dispute. The Supreme Court expressly left open Antrix's alternative defenses, including the impact of Indian courts setting aside the arbitral award on fraud grounds and whether the case should be dismissed on forum non conveniens grounds. These issues now return to the Ninth Circuit for consideration.

For the Indian diaspora and those following India's space industry, the case raises significant questions about the enforceability of international arbitration awards involving Indian government entities in foreign jurisdictions — and whether India's fraud findings will carry weight in American courts.
